title: AI giants want an antitrust exemption — is it safety or a cartel?
dek: Former DOJ antitrust chief Jonathan Cantor says building a safe product doesn't require coordinating with your rivals, just like Boeing doesn't need to check with Airbus when a door blows off — so no form of antitrust exemption should be granted.
why: High information density, but it's all legal and policy frameworks, no product details. Worth listening for anyone following AI regulation, antitrust, and US-China competition policy; skip it if you want model technology.
who: Founders, investors and policy researchers watching where AI regulation is heading, antitrust enforcement, and US-China tech competition policy.
skip: The sponsor read at the start, 0:00-0:30, and the production credits after 43:43 at the end.

points.h: Building a safe product doesn't require coordinating with rivals
points.body: Cantor splits AI safety into two questions: what companies should do, and what government should do. His core rebuttal is that companies don't need to coordinate to deliver a safe product — Boeing's door blowing off isn't Airbus's fault, and Boeing doesn't need to slow innovation down together with Airbus; a car exploding isn't another carmaker's fault. By the same logic, if your AI agent breaks into someone else's system, that's no different from sending an employee to do it, and the employer should be held liable. The only things that genuinely need collaboration are things like threat intelligence sharing, say a shared library of malicious bots, and antitrust law doesn't prohibit that kind of collaboration anyway. Antitrust law is only really triggered when two companies say "we're competing too hard, we need to slow down together."

points.h: Even the most charitable reading doesn't yield an exemption
points.body: Cantor offers two readings, from most charitable to most cynical, and both conclude no exemption should be granted. Most charitable: they genuinely fear the pace of innovation is out of control, there are no lines on the road, and they're afraid of driving off it or hitting someone, so they ask the government to step in — he believes they believe they might destroy humanity, but he doesn't think that doomsday scenario is accurate. Most cynical: they've burned so much money they can't sustain it, but pulling back would hit their valuations and IPOs, so they want someone to come out and give everyone a license to "slow down together," so they can figure out the economics before the election. He states plainly that neither reading should buy any form of antitrust exemption.

points.h: The products liability framework has already worked once
points.body: The host asks: if I direct my Meta agent to attack you, is that Meta's fault? Cantor says both — the company hires the people and builds the technology, and when people or technology go steal or break into someone else's property on the employer's behalf, liability exists, and it can be products liability or go beyond it. He cites Meta's case over child safety and mental health on Facebook and Instagram as an example, saying the products liability framework did recently work. But the host immediately points out: it took ten years to work, and that's the problem. Cantor concedes that, which is why government has to step in, and the pace of innovation is no excuse for not building a safe product.

points.h: Now liability should move from "maybe" to "certain"
points.body: The host proposes: Meta's products liability case ended in a settlement, Meta made concessions to regulators, but it took a long time. If today you said OpenAI will most likely be liable for ChatGPT's behavior and Anthropic will most likely be liable for Claude, shouldn't we tighten the screws now and legislate to say you are definitely liable? Cantor says that's exactly the clarifying work Congress should do, but today's environment is different from fifteen or twenty years ago: back then Section 230 gave online companies broad exemptions, plus a laissez-faire attitude starting in the Obama era, which let tech companies camp out directly in the White House and Congress and tell the government how to write the rules. He says that outcome has already destroyed public trust in these companies, which is why this conversation is happening much earlier — "fool me once, shame on you; fool me twice, shame on me."

points.h: Left and right are realigning on antitrust
points.body: The host points to a political realignment that confuses him: Trump's AI czar David Sacks retweeted former FTC chair Lina Khan, saying existing antitrust law is sufficient and no exemption is needed; hours later Bernie Sanders and Steve Bannon shared a stage in DC calling for a halt to AI development. Cantor calls this a "realignment of the realignment": in Trump's first term, left, right and center all worried about Big Tech power, and Lina and he took office with a popular mandate to enforce aggressively; the second term turned friendly first, and now the cracks are showing again. He adds that this kind of misalignment has existed for a while — when he testified in Congress he had support from Mike Lee, Chuck Grassley and Josh Hawley at the same time, and Matt Gaetz asked him at an oversight hearing, "Have you won enough?"

points.h: The China threat is a convenient shield
points.body: The host asks: these companies say America must win, otherwise the Chinese government will control AGI — is that a convenient boogeyman? Cantor says "to a large extent, yes." He goes back to the AT&T breakup: back then AT&T told the Reagan administration that winning the Cold War required a strong national telecommunications network, and the Reagan administration rejected that argument. He says the right way to compete with China is to play to America's strengths, and China isn't doing what we're doing — China restricts children's access to technology, censors information inside its borders, and concentrates control over companies through state-owned enterprises and affected firms. So the claim that "the only way to compete with China is to let us ship unsafe products" is absurd. He also says the lack of rules and accountability in the social media era actually led to a lack of innovation in "how to build products safer from the start."

points.h: Tolerating domestic monopoly for the sake of competing abroad is wrong
points.body: Cantor's framework is: drive fierce, dynamic competition inside the United States, including from foreign companies, because America is a market economy, and the chance of success is what motivates people to try new things, put in capital, and make good products. He says the idea that "we need domestic monopolies to compete abroad" is fundamentally opposed to the American way of life — America's founding itself was a revolt against British monopolies on the necessities of life. He acknowledges there are legitimate questions, such as how to handle foreign below-cost dumping, which this administration is raising; he mentions an 1980s case he read with law students: Japanese companies were accused of cartelizing and raising prices on televisions in Japan, then cross-subsidizing below-cost pricing in the US to crush domestic American manufacturers, and at the time the Supreme Court used an absurd set of economics to find this didn't constitute an antitrust violation. But he says the way to handle that problem is not to allow the domestic market to be monopolized.

points.h: NVIDIA's circular investments should be examined
points.body: The host asks on behalf of the most skeptical listeners: NVIDIA has circularly funded all these companies, and they're effectively already coordinated; the products liability theory will fall flat because OpenAI will never sue Hugging Face, and NVIDIA just bought Hugging Face and is also OpenAI's biggest investor — shouldn't all of this be broken apart? Cantor says "someone should be looking at these questions," which is exactly what they started doing in office: draw some lines, you can't buy whichever company you want or invest in whichever one you want, competition has to be competition, and within the boundaries you can compete as hard as you like. He criticizes this administration for allowing a handful of companies to reach dominant, oligopolistic or monopolistic positions in order to "beat China," but he asks back, "what does beating China even mean" — if China has advanced bots breaking into American companies and government servers, that's a national security, geopolitical, international relations problem, and it shouldn't be solved through domestic monopoly, especially when those monopolists owe loyalty to shareholders rather than the public interest.

points.h: Antitrust enforcement won cases and lost on remedies
points.body: Cantor sums up his tenure: they brought back aggressive enforcement, using theories that don't just look at whether consumer prices rise or fall, which was new at the time. They won against Google twice, the Apple case survived a motion to dismiss, the Ticketmaster case even won jury support when the Trump administration tried to settle, and they brought cases on algorithmic pricing and in healthcare. He concedes the remedy outcome in the Google case was disappointing, but that wasn't the part he presided over — he presided over the wins, then handed the baton to the next administration. Some people, especially in tech policy circles, say the whole thing was a failure that produced no structural change, and Cantor says "absolutely not": not finishing isn't failure, and it's inherently hard to act once a market has already hardened.

points.h: What you want to protect is the next inflection point
points.body: Cantor says he has always liked to say: what you really want to do is protect the next inflection point. Especially in technology and platforms, what comes next is likely to be highly disruptive, and competition is most promising at that moment — and that is exactly when incumbents are most aggressive about stopping new players from competing. The host picks up: you said the same thing last time you were on the show talking about the Apple case, that monopolists are most aggressive right before everything changes; Apple was the App Store, Google was bundling products in various ways. Now we're talking about challengers: Johnny Ive went to OpenAI to do hardware, and Apple is suing them. Cantor says yesterday's challengers are often today's monopolists, and he isn't against challengers — that's exactly why he's against antitrust exemptions; he wants challengers to keep charging hard, and he also wants thriving domestic open source or open weight models to compete.

points.h: The prescription: first make clear the cost of bad outcomes
points.body: Asked how he would prioritize if he were a policymaker, Cantor says start with "making clear the consequences of bad things": if you build a dangerous product, if the door blows off in midair, if your AI breaks into someone's company, you should be held liable, and you have an obligation to build a product that won't do that — this is an extension of the products liability-style framework, and it's a good starting point. Second, Congress should step in and enumerate the things society values: mental health, competition, the truthfulness of information, the intellectual property and copyright of content owners, and embed those values into the lines on the road, the stop signs and the traffic lights, so everyone knows from the start what's allowed and what isn't. He says maybe the next Congress can do it, and he hopes so.

quotes.text: So the state of the world right now is it's like we've invented cars and trucks, but we have no lines on the road, no traffic lights, and no stop signs and no speed limits.
So let me give you my interpretation from the most generous to the most cynical, neither of which, TLDR, should result in any sort of antitrust exemption.
These companies do not need to coordinate in order to deliver safe and secure products to society.
If you believe your product is going to destroy humanity, then don't build it.
The idea that we need monopolies at home in order to compete abroad is antithetical to our way of life.
China is a country of national champions. The United States is not a country of national champions.
And I've always been fond of saying that what you really want to do is you want to protect the next inflection point.
